before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the change-of-variables corollaries inside the proof of the retarded-convolution identity cited in clause (b) ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, let $v_*<c$, let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

(a) [Root and emission-time Jacobian] For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ (equivalently $x\ne z(t)$) there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. The map $s:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) one has $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad \nabla_xs(x,t)=-\frac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c],$$ so $\kappa\ge 1-v_*/c>0$ uniformly on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. Moreover, for the fixed $x$ and near the root, the function $s'\mapsto s'+|x-z(s')|/c$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with derivative $\kappa(x,t)$: this emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ is the denominator produced by the delta substitution of clause (b).

(b) [Delta substitution and Liénard-Wiechert potentials] Let $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the point-source distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] attached to $q$ and the worldline $z$, let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]], and for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$ and $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, exactly as in clause (b) of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]. Then these pairings are finite for every $\psi$ and their exact retarded-convolution values are $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt$$ (the second identity componentwise); equivalently, $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the $C^2$ functions $\varphi:=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A:=\beta\varphi/c$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. The weight $(\kappa r)^{-1}$ with $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ is the exact form of the substitution with denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$ (the rigorous statement is the displayed pairing identity; composition of $\delta$ with a function is not part of the distribution calculus used here).

(c) [Fields and the velocity/acceleration split] With $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]), and writing $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ at the root, $$E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{vel}}=\frac{C(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r},\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}$$ at every event of $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). Both $E$ and $B$ are continuous on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, and the velocity field obeys the bound $$|E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x,t)|\le C\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r(x,t)^{-2}$$ at every event.

(d) [Uniform far-zone remainder] For every $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and every $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|n|=1$, put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$ and $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and set $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\dot\beta_0:=z''(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$, and $$E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0\bigr)}{c\,\kappa_0^3\,r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r),\qquad B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c},$$ where the remainder is bounded uniformly in the direction, $$|\rho_E(s_0,n,r)|\le C\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r^{-2}\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2\text{ and every }r>0.$$ Equivalently, $rE(x_r,t_r)\to C\,n\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)/(c\,\kappa_0^3)$ as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over $n\in S^2$ at the explicit rate $O(r^{-1})$ given by the same bound multiplied by $r$. before.statement:
(i) [Plane-wave solutions with infinite spatial $L^2$ norm] Let $c>0$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as in [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function $u:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $u(x,t):=f(x_1-ct)$, is of class $C^\infty$ and satisfies $Wu=0$ identically. If $f\ne0$, then for every $t$ the level set $\{x:u(x,t)\ne0\}=(ct+U)\times\mathbb R^2$, where $U:=\{s\in\mathbb R:f(s)\ne0\}$ is nonempty and open, is unbounded, and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x,t)|^2\,dx=+\infty$. before.title: Causal convolution response, transfer function and dispersion relations
before.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#D1-D2 (compact and W^{1,1} integrable causal branches), assembled with the passivity quadratic form
before.statement:
Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$, and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous (absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$) with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ the relations hold with $\chi$ replaced by $\chi-\chi_\infty$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.
before.strategy:
Proof technique: direct, branch by branch; clausal tags below indicate the cited tools.

(a) For each $j$ and $t$, absolute convergence and the displayed bound follow from $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]). Linearity in $E$ is linearity of the integral. Continuity in $t$: if $t_n\to t$ then $K_{jk}(s)E_k(t_n-s)\to K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for every $s$ with the integrable dominating function $(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}|$, so dominated convergence gives $P(t_n)\to P(t)$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Causality: for $t\le t_0$ and every $s\ge0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so replacing $E$ by a history agreeing with it there changes no integrand value and hence no integral.

(b) Holomorphy is obtained from the real-parameter differentiation theorem rather than by differentiating in the complex variable directly. Writing $z=x+iy$, the integrand $K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}=K_{jk}(s)e^{ixs}e^{-ys}$ has continuous partials in $x$ and $y$; because $K_{jk}$ has compact support, on every compact set of parameters $(x,y)$ the partials are dominated by a fixed multiple of $|K_{jk}|(1+|s|)$, an integrable function, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied in the two real parameters gives the continuous partials $\partial_x\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). These satisfy $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=-\int sK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\int isK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy--Riemann equations for the pair $(\partial_x\chi_{jk},\partial_y\chi_{jk})$ with the identification $f=u+iv$; since the partials exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous, [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic, and because the same argument is available at every $z\in\mathbb C$, each entry is entire ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Iterating gives $\chi_{jk}^{(k)}(z)=\int_0^\infty(is)^kK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. For the reality identity at real $\omega$: conjugation is an isometry and a real-field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and the series defining the complex exponential converges everywhere ([[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]); conjugating the partial sums termwise and passing to the limit along the isometry gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$, so conjugating the defining integral of $\chi_{jk}$ and using that $K_{jk}$ is real gives $\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds=\chi_{jk}(-\omega)$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). Two integrations by parts with vanishing endpoint values, valid because $K$ vanishes near $0$ and at infinity, give $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the stated $|z|^{-2}$ bound ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]). For the dispersion relations fix real $\omega$ and form a contour consisting of the interval $[-R,R]$ indented above $\omega$ on a clockwise semicircle of radius $\delta$, closed by the large semicircle of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane; on the indented domain the integrand $\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops gives vanishing total integral ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]). The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\sup_{|z|=R}|\chi_{jk}|/R\to0$ by the $|z|^{-2}$ bound. The small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\to0$, by continuity of $\chi_{jk}$ on the closed upper half-plane, which follows from dominated convergence as in (a) ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. Letting $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating real and imaginary parts yields the displayed pair because $i(a+ib)=-b+ia$.

(c) This is precisely the content of the cited integrable-causal-dispersion lemma: that item proves, under exactly these hypotheses, the holomorphy on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]), the closed-half-plane bound, the boundary regularity and the two principal-value formulas, and records the instantaneous-response subtraction ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The present theorem assembles the response, its transfer function and the passivity relation around that lemma; no additional proof obligation is created here.

(d) The period-average of a product of real parts of complex exponentials is supplied by [[lem-em-period-average]], which states exactly $\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\cdot\overline d)$; applying it with $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ (the derivative of $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, computed with the chain rule) gives $$\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e\cdot\overline{(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e}\Bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),$$ using $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). Finally $e^*M(\omega)e=(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e)/(2i)=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ because $M(\omega)$ is the Hermitian part of $\chi(\omega)$, so nonnegativity of the displayed average for every $e$ is exactly the stated quadratic-form condition. The logical independence of causality and this positivity (the design's 'no sign of dissipation follows merely from causality') is exhibited on the companion example page by a kernel satisfying (c) whose quadratic form is strictly negative.

before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the surface-integral conventions used by [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]].

(i) (Causality without passivity.) Let $K(s):=-e^{-s}$ for $s\ge0$. Then $K$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ (indeed $K'=e^{-s}=-K$, $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$), so the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] applies: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories, its transfer function is $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and its boundary value $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$. Hence the Hermitian part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative, not positive semidefinite, and the monochromatic period-averaged work of clause (d) of that theorem is strictly negative for $d=1$, every $e\ne0$ and every $\omega>0$ (with any response normalization $\varepsilon_0>0$), although the response is causal and its entry satisfies the dispersion relations of clause (c). Nonnegative period-averaged work (passivity) is therefore an additional condition on the model, not a consequence of temporal causality.

(ii) (The flux limit needs fixed retarded time.) In the setting of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]], fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in S^2$, and let $r>\max\{2a,\;a+c(t-t_0)\}$. Then for every $y\in B_a$ one has $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, so $t-R/c<t_0$; by hypothesis (H1) of that theorem the functions $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$, so every integrand in the field formulas of clause (a) of that theorem vanishes and $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, hence $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. Therefore $\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$: at fixed observation time the far-zone flux integral is identically zero beyond the light cone of the compact spacetime support, whereas clause (c) of that theorem is a limit at fixed retarded time. The retarded-time formulation cannot be replaced by a fixed-observation-time one.

Nothing is asserted for a finite-history trajectory, for a trajectory whose speed approaches $c$ without a uniform bound, or about the complete retarded field formula of the causal-response page.
before.strategy: Define $f(s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ on $\mathbb R$ (for the fixed pair $(x,t)$). It is continuous, $f(t)<0$ because $x\ne z(t)$, and $|z(s)|\le|z(0)|+v_*|s|$ makes $f(s)\to+\infty$ as $s\to-\infty$. For $s_2>s_1$ the integral representation of $z(s_2)-z(s_1)$ together with the integral triangle inequality ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) gives $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*(s_2-s_1)$, hence $f(s_2)-f(s_1)\le-(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)<0$: $f$ is strictly decreasing. The intermediate value theorem ([[thm-intermediate-value]]) and strict decrease give one root, strictly below $t$. At that root $r=c(t-s)>0$, so $|x-z(\cdot)|$ is a composition of smooth maps on a neighbourhood of $s$ and $\partial_sf=-\kappa\le-(1-v_*/c)<0$ is bounded away from zero uniformly. The parametrized implicit function theorem with $C^k$ regularity ([[thm-parametrized-implicit-function-theorem-with-higher-regularity]]) applied to $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ gives $C^3$ regularity of $s(x,t)$ and the derivative formula $Ds=-F_s^{-1}D_{(x,t)}F$; differentiating $f=0$ gives $\partial_ts=\kappa^{-1}$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$.

after.title: Global existence, uniqueness and differentiability of the retarded root
after.statement: Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.
after.strategy: The ordinary vector FTC and integral triangle inequality give $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$. For fixed $x$ put $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$. It is continuous and for $s_2>s_1$ satisfies $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\ge(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)>0$. Consequently $g_x(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$; IVT and strict monotonicity give a unique solution of $g_x(s)=t$. Since $g_x(s)\ge s$, $s\le t$, and equality is equivalent to $x=z(t)$. On $D$ the root has $r>0$. Continuity of $z$ makes $D$ open. Near any root on $D$, $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ has precisely the regularity of $z$, because the Euclidean norm is smooth away from zero. Its $s$ derivative is $-\kappa$, bounded away from zero. Apply the parametrized implicit-function theorem with its actual $C^1$ hypothesis first, or with $C^k$ when $z$ is $C^k$; global uniqueness glues these local maps. Differentiating $F=0$ gives the two stated formulas. Repeat for every finite $k$ in the smooth case. Do not infer $C^3$ from $C^1$, and do not exclude an observation point merely because the trajectory visits it at a different time. The exact non-improvement witness is a small uniformly subluminal $z(s)=(\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2},0,0)$ with smooth compact cutoff $\chi=1$ near zero. At a distant positive axial point $L>\sup|z|$, the retardation map is $g(s)=s+(L-\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2})/c$, $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at zero. A $C^2$ inverse near $t=L/c$, whose derivative is nonzero, would make $g$ $C^2$ by the inverse-function theorem, a contradiction.

before.title: Dispersion relations for an absolutely continuous integrable causal kernel
before.statement: Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let $$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$ be the matrix response function. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$ An instantaneous real response matrix may be added as $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, in which case the formulas apply to $\chi-\chi_\infty$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.
before.strategy: Absolute integrability bounds each entry of $\chi$ on the closed upper half-plane, and continuity is by dominated convergence ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge\delta>0$ the parameter derivatives have the integrable entrywise bound $|s\,e^{izs}|\le s\,e^{-\delta s}$, so differentiation under the integral sign ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]) gives holomorphy of each entry; the hypothesis $sK\in L^1$ makes the entrywise first derivative continuous on the real boundary. Local absolute continuity with $K'\in L^1$ and $K\in L^1$ gives $K(s)\to0$ at infinity (as a matrix), and entrywise integration by parts ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]) gives $\chi(z)=-K(0)/(iz)-(iz)^{-1}\int_0^\infty K'(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the uniform entrywise bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le[|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1]/|z|$. Apply Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]], with complex line integrals along closed rectifiable contours, [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]) to each entry of $\chi(z)/(z-\omega)$ on the indented upper-semicircle domain (a small semicircular indentation around the real point $\omega$ and a large half-circle of radius $R$). The large-arc integrand is $O(R^{-2})$ on length $\pi R$ and tends to zero; the indentation contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating the remaining real-axis principal values gives the displayed pair of formulas entrywise, the $O(|\xi|^{-1})+C^1$ control of the tail ensuring the principal values exist. The matrix form reduces to the scalar form in each entry, and $\chi_\infty$ is handled by subtracting it before the contour argument.

after.title: Dispersion relations for an absolutely continuous integrable causal kernel
after.statement: Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let $$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$ be the matrix response function. Here locally absolutely continuous means that each real entry restricted to every compact interval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\infty)$ satisfies the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\sum_\ell(v_\ell-u_\ell)<\delta$ implies $\sum_\ell|K_{jk}(v_\ell)-K_{jk}(u_\ell)|<\epsilon$ for every finite family with disjoint interiors. $K\prime$ denotes the almost-everywhere derivative, with any measurable zero extension on its null exceptional set. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$ The sharper bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K\prime_{jk}\|_1)/|z|$ holds for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. Here $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ means $\lim_{R\to\infty}\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}(\int_{\omega-R}^{\omega-\eta}+\int_{\omega+\eta}^{\omega+R})F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$; the tails converge absolutely, so the choice of centering at infinity does not change the limit. For an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define the total transfer function $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$; the formulas then apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.
after.strategy:
Treat each real entry $k=K_{jk}$ separately. Its locally absolutely continuous representative is the one in the statement; the published [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] applies on $[0,N]$ under the declared Countable Choice and Dependent Choice and yields $k(s)=k(0)+\int_0^s k\prime(u)du$. Since $k\prime\in L^1$, dominated convergence shows this has a finite limit $\ell=k(0)+\int_0^\infty k\prime$. If $\ell\ne0$, then $|k(s)|\ge|\ell|/2$ for all sufficiently large $s$, contradicting $k\in L^1$ by monotonicity of the integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Hence $k(s)\to0$.
The defining integral is bounded by $\|k\|_1$ on $\overline H$, and dominated convergence gives joint continuity there ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Writing $z=x+iy$, the real parameter derivatives of $k(s)e^{izs}$ are $isk(s)e^{izs}$ and $-sk(s)e^{izs}$. On any rectangle in $H$ their absolute values are bounded by $s|k(s)|$, integrable by hypothesis. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied separately in $x,y$ supplies the partials; dominated convergence makes them continuous, and $\partial_y\chi=i\partial_x\chi$ gives holomorphy by [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]]. Along the real boundary the same theorem in the real parameter and the same majorant give the continuous derivative $\chi\prime(\omega)=\int_0^\infty isk(s)e^{i\omega s}ds$.
For fixed $z\ne0$, the real and imaginary parts of $g(s):=e^{izs}$ are $C^1$ on each $[0,N]$, hence absolutely continuous by [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]. Apply [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] separately to $(k,\operatorname{Re}g)$ and $(k,\operatorname{Im}g)$ and combine the real identities to get
$$\int_0^N k(s)e^{izs}ds=\frac{k(N)e^{izN}-k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^N k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds.$$
This is Lebesgue integration by parts for AC functions, not the ordinary everywhere-differentiable Riemann theorem. For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, $|e^{izs}|\le1$; $k(N)\to0$ kills the endpoint term and dominated convergence applies to both integrals. Thus
$$\chi_{jk}(z)=-\frac{k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^\infty k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds,\qquad |\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\frac{|k(0)|+\|k\prime\|_1}{|z|}.$$
For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $F$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $F(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $F(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $F$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $F(z+i\delta)\to F(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $F(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi F(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[F(\xi)-F(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi F(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply the preceding step to each entry of $\chi$. Adding the stipulated real instantaneous matrix means the total transfer function is $\chi_\infty+\chi$; subtract $\chi_\infty$ before taking the principal values. All scalar claims are the $d=1$ case. Neither temporal causality nor these analytic identities impose the separate passivity quadratic-form condition.

before.title: Dispersion relations for a finitely subtracted analytic response
before.statement: Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). Let $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)(z-\omega_0)^j/j!$ be the Taylor polynomial at $\omega_0$ and $f(z)=[\chi(z)-P(z)]/(z-\omega_0)^n$, with the removable value at $\omega_0$. Assume the boundary restriction of $f$ is class $C^1$ (the local holomorphy supplies this at $\omega_0$). Then for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Re}P(\omega)+\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$ and the corresponding imaginary formula holds with the minus Hilbert transform of $\operatorname{Re}f$ plus $\operatorname{Im}P$. At $\omega=\omega_0$ the formula is read as the stated Taylor value. An explicit constitutive response given by a real polynomial in time derivatives plus an integrable causal kernel satisfies these formulas with the polynomial subtraction identified; general passivity and storage remain separate model conditions.
before.strategy: The Taylor factorization makes $f$ holomorphic through $\omega_0$ ([[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]], [[def-complex-domain]]); elsewhere $f$ is holomorphic in the upper half-plane because the denominator is nonzero. The growth assumption and the polynomial degree give $f(z)=O(|z|^{-1})$ uniformly on the upper large semicircle, and its $C^1$ boundary controls the principal-value divided difference while its tail divided by $\xi-\omega$ is integrable. The indented contour argument of the integrable-causal-dispersion lemma ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]], whose proof applies Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops, [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]) applies verbatim to $f$ and yields the pair of dispersion formulas for $f$; multiplying by the real factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$ and adding $P$ gives the stated formulas, and the removable Taylor identity at $\omega_0$ gives the declared value there. A complex Taylor polynomial cannot be deleted from the imaginary numerator: it is subtracted only through the displayed $P$.

after.title: Dispersion relations for a finitely subtracted analytic response
after.statement: Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane and continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). Let $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)(z-\omega_0)^j/j!$ be the Taylor polynomial at $\omega_0$ and $f(z)=[\chi(z)-P(z)]/(z-\omega_0)^n$, with the removable value at $\omega_0$. Assume the boundary restriction of $f$ is class $C^1$ (the local holomorphy supplies this at $\omega_0$). Then for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Re}P(\omega)+\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$ $$\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}P(\omega)-\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi.$$ At $\omega=\omega_0$ the formula is read as the stated Taylor value. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is also valid with $P=0$, $f=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and the factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ for all $\omega$; at $\omega_0$ use the same principal-value formula rather than a Taylor-value convention. For the separate constitutive polynomial branch assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]), let $A_0,\ldots,A_m$ be real scalar coefficients or real matrices, and let $K$ satisfy all hypotheses of [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]. On histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$, the response $\sum_{j=0}^m A_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal, and its transfer function in the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z):=\sum_{j=0}^m A_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared polynomial $Q$ leaves the proved entrywise dispersion formulas for $\chi_K$; this branch does not require holomorphic continuation through a real subtraction point. The Taylor-subtracted formulas above apply to the total response when its additional local-holomorphy, growth and boundary hypotheses are satisfied; $Q$ need not equal its Taylor polynomial $P$. General passivity and storage remain separate model conditions.
after.strategy:
[[thm-taylor-expansion-holomorphic-function]] on a complex neighborhood of $\omega_0$ shows that $\chi-P$ has a zero of order at least $n$, so division gives the holomorphic removable continuation of $f$ there. Elsewhere in $H$ its denominator is nonzero. Continuity of $\chi$ on $\overline H$ and the removable continuation make $f$ continuous on $\overline H$; its real restriction is $C^1$ by hypothesis. The growth bound on $\chi$ and the degree of $P$ give $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly in $\overline H$ at infinity. For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $f$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $f(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $f$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $f(z+i\delta)\to f(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $f(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi f(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[f(\xi)-f(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi f(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply that boundary-contour argument to $f$, multiply both formulas by the real factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$, and add the complex polynomial $P$. At $\omega_0$ the factor vanishes and the removable Taylor identity gives the asserted Taylor value. The imaginary numerator subtracts the full complex $P$; it cannot be omitted.
For the distinct constitutive branch, multiplication by $(-i\omega)^j$ is the derivative multiplier on the stipulated monochromatic histories, so the transfer polynomial is exactly $Q$. Derivatives at a time are determined by a history agreeing on its whole past, including its endpoint, and the convolution is causal; hence their finite sum is causal on histories with the stated bounded continuous derivatives. The residual $\chi-Q=\chi_K$ satisfies [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]] entrywise. Without that lemma's AC and integrability conditions a merely integrable causal kernel still gives a bounded upper-half-plane holomorphic response, but does not automatically supply these principal values or Taylor continuation. The stated additional analytic assumptions, not causality alone, govern the Taylor branch.

before.title: A closed 1-form on a simply connected open subset of the affine model has a primitive
before.statement: Let U be a nonempty open subset of A which, with the manifold topology of lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas, is path-connected and simply connected (def-simply-connected), and let alpha be a C^1 one-form on U with d alpha = 0 (def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms). Then there is a C^2 function F: U -> R with dF = alpha. Consequently, for any two piecewise C^1 paths gamma_0, gamma_1 in U with the same endpoints the integrals of alpha along them are equal, and the integral of alpha along every piecewise C^1 loop in U vanishes.
before.strategy: Complete elementary argument by grid approximation of a based null-homotopy; it needs no smoothing theorem and no choice principle. (i) Let gamma be a piecewise C^1 loop in U based at p_0 and let H: [0,1]x[0,1] -> U be a based null-homotopy (H(.,0) = gamma, H(.,1) = p_0, H(0,s) = H(1,s) = p_0; def-nullhomotopic-map-and-contractible-space, def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy). (ii) The image H([0,1]^2) is compact (thm-heine-borel-rn in an inertial chart); cover it by finitely many convex open coordinate boxes contained in U (for each point take a small Euclidean ball inside U). By uniform continuity of H on the compact square (thm-heine-cantor-metric) there is a grid 0 = t_0 < ... < t_N = 1 such that the image of every cell [t_i,t_{i+1}]x[s_j,s_{j+1}] lies in one of the boxes B_{ij}. (iii) On each convex box alpha = d phi_{ij} by the Poincare lemma for star-shaped domains (thm-poincare-lemma-for-differential-forms-on-star-shaped-domains), and for every piecewise C^1 path in the box from a to b the integral of alpha is phi_{ij}(b) - phi_{ij}(a) (thm-chain-rule and thm-ftc-first-part on each smooth piece; def-piecewise-c1-path-connected-conservative-and-path-independent). (iv) Replace the bottom image H(.,0) = gamma by the polygonal path through the grid vertices: on each interval [t_i,t_{i+1}] the arc gamma|[t_i,t_{i+1}] and the straight chord joining its endpoints both lie in B_{i0} (the first by construction, the second by convexity), so the two integrals agree; the top side is the constant path and the two vertical sides are constant, so their integrals vanish. (v) Let H' be the map that is bilinear on each cell and agrees with H at the cell corners; it is well defined (on shared edges both cells interpolate linearly between the same two corner values) and continuous. Its boundary curve Gamma is a closed polygonal curve in U, and the sum of the boundary integrals of alpha over all cells equals the integral over Gamma because interior edges cancel. Each cell boundary is a closed piecewise C^1 quadrilateral lying in the convex box B_{ij}, so its integral is phi_{ij}(q_1) - phi_{ij}(q_1) = 0 by (iii) with the four sides telescoping. Hence the integral of alpha over Gamma vanishes, and by (iv) the integral over gamma vanishes as well. (vi) For two piecewise C^1 paths gamma_0, gamma_1 from p to q the concatenation gamma_0 * (gamma_1 reversed) is a piecewise C^1 loop at p, null-homotopic because U is simply connected, so its integral vanishes and the integrals along gamma_0 and gamma_1 are equal. (vii) Fix p_0 in U and define F(x) as the integral of alpha along any piecewise C^1 path from p_0 to x; (vi) makes this well defined. For a small coordinate ball around x inside U, F(x+h e_i) - F(x) equals the integral along the straight segment from x to x+h e_i, and the difference-quotient limit is alpha_i(x) by continuity of the components; hence F is C^1 with dF = alpha, and F is C^2 because alpha is C^1. All selections are finite.

after.title: A closed 1-form on a simply connected open subset of the affine model has a primitive
after.statement: Let U be a nonempty open subset of A which, with the manifold topology of lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas, is path-connected and simply connected (def-simply-connected), and let alpha be a C^1 one-form on U with d alpha = 0 (def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms). Then there is a C^2 function F: U -> R with dF = alpha. Consequently, for any two piecewise C^1 paths gamma_0, gamma_1 in U with the same endpoints the integrals of alpha along them are equal, and the integral of alpha along every piecewise C^1 loop in U vanishes. Here for a C^1 one-form, closedness means in an inertial chart alpha=sum_i a_i dx^i with partial_i a_j=partial_j a_i; the exterior derivative is understood by this coefficient formula. If alpha is smooth, F may be taken smooth.
after.strategy:
Fix one inertial affine chart, identifying U with an open subset of R^4, and write alpha=sum_i a_i dx^i. Closedness for a C^1 form means partial_i a_j=partial_j a_i. All integration below is ordinary integration along finitely piecewise-C^1 paths.
(1) Local C^1 primitive, supplied in full rather than invoking the smooth-only imported Poincare theorem. On any convex ball B contained in U, fix b in B and set phi(x)=integral_0^1 sum_i a_i(b+t(x-b))(x_i-b_i) dt. For x in B and sufficiently small h, the radial segments for x+h e_j lie in a compact subset of B. The parameter derivative of the integrand is continuous on that compact set. The one-variable FTC expresses its difference quotient as the average of that derivative along x+u h e_j; uniform continuity makes these averages converge uniformly in t. Hence taking the integral of the quotient gives partial_j phi(x)=integral_0^1 [a_j(b+t(x-b))+t sum_i (x_i-b_i) partial_j a_i(b+t(x-b))]dt. Closedness and the chain rule identify the integrand with d/dt[t a_j(b+t(x-b))], so FTC gives partial_j phi=a_j. These partial derivatives are continuous, hence phi is C^1; since all a_j are C^1, phi is C^2. Chain rule and FTC on each path piece give integral_gamma alpha=phi(gamma(1))-phi(gamma(0)) for every piecewise-C^1 path contained in B. This is the C^1 radial proof of Lebl Thm 9.3.6, written explicitly here.
(2) Compact small-cell construction. Given a continuous based null-homotopy H:[0,1]^2 -> U of a piecewise-C^1 loop gamma at p, compactness of K=H([0,1]^2) gives finitely many balls B(b_l,r_l) contained in U whose concentric half-radius balls cover K. To obtain this finite family, cover K by all pairs of such balls centered at points of K; use compactness, then finitely many witnesses. Set r=min_l r_l>0. Uniform continuity of H gives delta>0 such that domain distances less than delta imply image distances less than r/2. Choose a finite rectangular mesh with cell diameter less than delta. For each cell, its lower-left image vertex belongs to a half-radius ball; the entire cell image is therefore contained in the corresponding full-radius ball. Only finitely many ball assignments are made. Refine the bottom mesh by the finitely many breakpoints of gamma if desired; this preserves the small-cell property.
(3) Replace each oriented mesh edge by the affine straight segment between its two image vertices. Each cell's four segments lie in its assigned convex ball, so its boundary integral is zero by (1). Every shared edge is exactly the same segment traversed oppositely by the adjacent cell; therefore finite summation cancels all interior edges. The top and vertical boundary segments are constant, since the homotopy is based. Each bottom loop arc and its replacement chord lie in the ball assigned to the corresponding bottom cell, so (1) makes their integrals equal. Thus integral_gamma alpha=0. No differentiability of H or smoothing theorem is used. The argument needs only continuous based null-homotopies, which the simply-connected definition supplies at every basepoint.
(4) For any two piecewise-C^1 paths from p to q, concatenate the first with the reversed second. It is a loop with zero integral by (3); finite concatenation and reversal give equal integrals. Piecewise-C^1 paths between points actually exist: take any continuous path, cover its compact image by finitely many half-radius balls inside U, apply uniform continuity and a finite subdivision as in (2), and replace the successive arcs by chords lying in the full balls. The resulting polygonal path stays in U and has the same endpoints.
(5) Fix p0 in the nonempty U. For each x let F(x) be the unique real value of the integral over a piecewise-C^1 path from p0 to x; existence follows from (4), and path independence makes the value unique. This defines F by a unique-value relation, without choosing a path simultaneously for every x. For any ball B around x contained in U, (1) and path concatenation give F(y)=F(x)+phi(y)-phi(x) for y in B. Therefore F is C^2 and dF=alpha on U. If alpha is smooth, repeated differentiation of partial_j F=a_j makes F smooth. Loop-integral vanishing and path independence were proved in (3)-(4). No AC or countable-choice principle is used. All existential path/homotopy choices concern a single object at a time, all mesh/ball choices are finite, and the global F uses uniqueness rather than a family of selected representatives.

before.title: Counterexample: a Born-rigid congruence need not be a Killing congruence
before.statement: Statement refuted: 'every smooth Born-rigid future unit timelike field n is locally a positive multiple of a Killing field'. Fix a length scale L_0>0 and use a geometric proper-length parameter lambda (the model's proper-time parameter is tau=lambda/c). Put psi(lambda)=lambda^2/(2L_0^2), e_0(lambda)=(cosh psi,sinh psi,0,0), e_1(lambda)=(sinh psi,cosh psi,0,0), and z(lambda)=(integral_0^lambda cosh psi(s) ds,integral_0^lambda sinh psi(s) ds,0,0), so z'=e_0 and eta(z',z')=-1. Define Phi(lambda,xi,y,zeta)=z(lambda)+xi e_1(lambda)+y e_2+zeta e_3. On a sufficiently small open coordinate box around0 this is injective with smooth inverse and N=1+k(lambda)xi>0, where k(lambda)=lambda/L_0^2; its pullback metric is -N^2 d lambda^2+d xi^2+dy^2+d zeta^2. The unit field n=N^-1 partial_lambda is future, irrotational and Born rigid: its rest slices lambda=const have fixed Euclidean induced metric. Its acceleration one-form is a-flat=[k(lambda)/N]d xi, and d(a-flat)=[1/(L_0^2N^2)]d lambda wedge d xi is nowhere zero. For a positive smooth f, the Killing equation for K=f n and Born rigidity imply d log f=a-flat, impossible because d^2 log f=0. Thus no positive smooth multiple of this n is Killing even locally; irrotational Born rigidity does not force a Killing rescaling. The Rindler congruence is not this counterexample: rho n=partial_theta is Killing for its theta-independent metric. The rotational classification of thm-sr-smooth-local-herglotz-noether is preserved; this example concerns its irrotational branch.
before.strategy: The hyperbolic identities give an orthonormal pair (e_0,e_1), with e_0'=k e_1 and e_1'=k e_0. The FTC defines z'=e_0. Differentiating Phi gives partial_lambda Phi=N e_0, partial_xi Phi=e_1 and the constant transverse vectors; at0 the derivative is invertible, so the choice-free smooth inverse-function theorem gives an injective local chart. Shrink to a coordinate box with |lambda|,|xi|<epsilon L_0 and epsilon<1 to ensure N>=1-epsilon^2>0. The metric follows directly; its rest-slice metric is lambda-independent, so theta=0, and its rest distribution is the lambda foliation, so omega=0. Its Christoffel/flat-coordinate derivative gives a=(k/N)partial_xi, hence a-flat=(k/N)d xi. Differentiate k/(1+k xi) in lambda: k'/N^2=1/(L_0^2N^2), proving the displayed nonclosed acceleration form. For Born-rigid n, sym nabla n=-n-flat sym-tensor a-flat. The equation L_{f n}eta=0 is n-flat sym-tensor(df-f a-flat)=0; evaluation twice on n and once on n plus a rest vector forces df-f a-flat=0, hence d log f=a-flat. Applying d and the exterior-square-zero theorem contradicts the everywhere nonzero displayed two-form. This replaces the false Rindler counterexample while preserving the full intended claim. Its explicit local construction has no global quotient, tube completeness or material-model assumption, and uses no choice principle.

before.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
before.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ with graph contained in an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$. For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_Iz'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,$$ the integrands having compact support in $I$. Then $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$.
before.strategy: Pair the divergence with a test: $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]\,dt=-q\int_I\frac{d}{dt}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt=0$, since $t\mapsto\psi(z(t),t)$ is $C^1$ with compact support. The chain rule supplies the derivative. Only prescribed point support is proved; Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted.

after.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
after.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ open containing its graph. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$, $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$, is proper: the inverse image of every compact subset of $\Omega$ is compact in $I$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_I z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. These define distributions and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, or if $I=\mathbb R$. Endpoint variant: if $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite, and both endpoint events belong to $\Omega$, the same integrals instead define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)}$. A finite-history source is source-free only when the endpoint contribution vanishes on the chosen test domain; neither mere graph containment nor test compactness alone supplies this.
after.strategy: For a fixed compact test support $K\subset\Omega$, properness makes $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ compact in $I$. It lies in one closed interior interval $[u,v]\subset I$, on which $z'$ is bounded. Both pairings are bounded by constants depending on $K$ times $\sup_K|\psi|$, proving distribution continuity on each test-support space. The pullback of a test is $C^1$ and compactly supported in $I$. By the total chain rule, pairing the divergence gives $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]dt=-q\int_I(d/dt)\psi(z(t),t)dt=0$ by interior FTC. For $I=\mathbb R$, compact ambient support bounds the time coordinate and its graph preimage is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R$; for $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, compact ambient support has time projection compact inside $I$. This proves both automatic properness claims. In the endpoint variant, finite interval length and the finite absolute improper integral of $z'$ bound the pairings on every compact test support. Apply the chain rule and FTC on $[a+\epsilon,b-\epsilon]$; the derivative pullback is absolutely integrable, and continuity at endpoints gives the limiting identity $q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)$. This proves the two endpoint deltas. In particular $I=(0,1),z=0,\Omega=\mathbb R^4$ gives $q\delta_{(0,0)}-q\delta_{(0,1)}$, refuting the old unconditional claim. The endpoint integration limit is explicitly this truncation argument, not an invented source reading. Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted. Here the two-ended improper integral means the sum of the limits of integrals on [a+epsilon,r] and [r,b−epsilon] for any fixed interior r. Monotonicity and completeness prove convergence of every nonnegative integrand bounded by a constant times 1+|z′|; signed limits then follow from the positive and negative parts. Thus the endpoint variant uses only the explicitly supplied improper convention and truncated ordinary FTC.

before.title: Retarded Liénard-Wiechert potentials and fields of a uniformly subluminal smooth point source
before.statement: Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the distributions $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Then the pairings $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$$ are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the smooth functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the distribution $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\varphi$, $\Upsilon$ that of $A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline, $$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$ The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.

after.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the distributions $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals
$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad
\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds.$$
Here the second integral is componentwise. The notation $\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$ and $\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, if used, means precisely these explicit history integrals, rather than ordinary distribution action on a compactly supported test. These pairings define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the $C^2$ functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the zero extensions $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\widetilde\varphi$, and $\Upsilon$ that of $\widetilde A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline, $$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$ The fields $E,B$ are $C^1$ off the worldline. More generally, if $z\in C^k$, $k\ge3$, the retarded root is $C^k$, the potentials are $C^{k-1}$ and the fields are $C^{k-2}$ there; if $z\in C^\infty$, all these objects are smooth off the worldline. The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.
after.strategy:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as stipulated in the statement. (a) Apply [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] to the $C^1$ curve $z$ on $\mathbb R$; $C^3$ is a special case, and its all-time graph is proper because a compact ambient set bounds the time coordinate.
(b) Fix a compact observation set $Q\subseteq\{(x,t):|x|\le M,\ t_0\le t\le t_1\}$, and tests supported in $Q$. If $g(s,y):=(z(s)+y,s+|y|/c)\in Q$, then $s\le t_1$. For $s\le0$, using $|z(s)|\le Z+v_*|s|$ with $Z:=|z(0)|$ gives
$$t_0\le s+|y|/c=s+|x-z(s)|/c\le -(1-v_*/c)|s|+(M+Z)/c.$$
Thus $s\ge-S$, where $S:=\max\{0,(M+Z-ct_0)/(c-v_*)\}$. If $[-S,t_1]$ is empty no contributing point exists. Otherwise set $H:=\max(S,|t_1|)$ and $L:=1+M+Z+v_*H$. Every contributing $y$ has $|y|\le M+|z(s)|<L$. Consequently the pulled-back support lies in the bounded closed cylinder $[-S,t_1]\times\overline B_L$, possibly approaching $y=0$; it need not be compact inside $U:=\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.
On that cylinder, $|\psi(g(s,y))|/(4\pi|y|)\le\|\psi\|_\infty/(4\pi|y|)$. The polar formula [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] gives $\int_{B_L}|y|^{-1}dy=\sigma(S^2)L^2/2<\infty$. Borel product identification [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] and the Euclidean/product-measure bridge [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] allow [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] for the absolute value. Then [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] identifies the double integral with the explicit iterated history integral. In particular, with $T:=\max(0,t_1+S)$ and $M_Q:=T\sigma(S^2)L^2/(8\pi)$,
$$|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|\le |q|M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty/\varepsilon_0,\qquad
|\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle|\le\mu_0|q|v_*M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty.$$
The seminorm $\psi\mapsto|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|$ restricts continuously to each fixed-support test space by these bounds, and likewise for each component of $\Upsilon$. Thus [[def-test-function-topology]] and [[def-distribution]] prove distribution continuity directly; no action of $\rho$ or $J$ on a noncompact test is assumed.
The graph $\Gamma$ is closed: convergence of $(z(s_j),s_j)$ forces $s_j\to t$ and $z(s_j)\to z(t)$. Thus $V:=\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ is open. On $U$, $g$ is $C^1$, and in coordinate order $(s,y_1,y_2,y_3)$ its determinant is $-\kappa(s,y)$, with $\kappa=1-(y/|y|)\cdot z'(s)/c\ge1-v_*/c>0$. If $g(s,y)=g(s',y')$, then $|s-s'|=||y'|-|y||/c\le|z(s')-z(s)|/c\le(v_*/c)|s-s'|$, so $s=s'$ and $y=y'$. No image point belongs to $\Gamma$: otherwise $|y|=|z(t)-z(s)|\le v_*(t-s)=v_*|y|/c$, contradicting $y\ne0$. Conversely every point of $V$ has the unique retarded root supplied by [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]], giving inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(s(x,t),x-z(s(x,t)))$. Its $C^1$ regularity follows from that supplier's $C^3$ branch on the open domain $x\ne z(t)$, using this consumer's $C^3$ hypothesis. No exclusion of the entire spatial trajectory is imposed. Therefore $g:U\to V$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.
For any compact $Q\subseteq\Omega$, the nonnegative Borel substitution lemma [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]] applied to $1_Q/(\kappa r)$ on $V$ yields
$$\int_V\frac{1_Q}{\kappa r}\,dx\,dt=\int_U\frac{1_Q(g(s,y))}{|y|}\,ds\,dy<\infty.$$
The same bound holds for $|\beta|/(c\kappa r)$ since $|\beta|\le v_*/c$. Extend the potentials by zero on the closed graph. These extensions are Borel and locally integrable on all of $\Omega$. Applying the same Borel substitution first to the absolute value of $\psi/(\kappa r)$ establishes its $L^1$ integrability on $V$, and [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]] then gives the scalar pairing formula in the statement. Apply it componentwise to $z'(s)$-weighted data for the vector formula. Its prefactor is
$$\frac{\mu_0qz'(s)}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0qc\beta}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0c\varepsilon_0 C\beta}{\kappa r}=\frac{C\beta}{c\kappa r},$$
since $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$. The regular-distribution identities mean the zero extensions, as in [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]; tests may be nonzero on $\Gamma$. The retarded root is $C^3$ on $V$, and $r,n$ are $C^3$ while $\beta,\kappa,D$ are $C^2$ with $D>0$, so the potentials are $C^2$. The same composition argument gives the matching $C^k$ and $C^\infty$ branches.
(c) Derivatives of the retarded data: from $t-s=r/c$ and R1, $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$, $s_t=1/\kappa$, hence $\nabla r=n/\kappa$ and $r_t=-cN/\kappa$ (chain rule, [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); $R=x-z(s)$ gives $\partial_iR=e_i+\beta\,n_i/\kappa$ and $\beta=z'(s)/c$ gives $\partial_i\beta=-\dot\beta\,n_i/(c\kappa)$, while $\beta_t=\dot\beta/\kappa$ (componentwise chain rule and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Since $D=r-R\cdot\beta$, the product rules for the Euclidean pairing give $D_t=r_t-R_t\cdot\beta-R\cdot\beta_t=(c(|\beta|^2-N)-rd)/\kappa$ and $\partial_iD=\partial_ir-(\partial_iR)\cdot\beta-R\cdot\partial_i\beta$, hence $\nabla D=((1-|\beta|^2+rd/c)/\kappa)\,n-\beta$; the required product rules are the coordinatewise one-variable product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then $\varphi=C/D$ gives $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$, $\varphi_t=-CD_t/D^2$, and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ gives $A_t=(\beta_t\varphi+\beta\varphi_t)/c=\dot\beta C/(c\kappa D)-\beta CD_t/(cD^2)$, so $$E=-\nabla\varphi-A_t=\frac{C}{D^2}\Bigl(\nabla D+\frac{\beta D_t}{c}\Bigr)-\frac{C\dot\beta}{c\kappa D}.$$ The bracket equals $\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+(rd/c)(n-\beta)}{\kappa}$ (substituting the two displayed identities and $\kappa=1-N$), and writing the second term over the common denominator $\kappa^3r^2$ replaces its numerator by $-r\kappa\dot\beta/c$, giving $E=\frac{C}{\kappa^3r^2}\bigl[(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+\frac{r}{c}\bigl(d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta\bigr)\bigr]$; the coordinate triple-product identity $n\times((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta)=d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta$ (expand both sides with [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]) yields the displayed $E$. For the magnetic field, $\operatorname{curl}(\beta\varphi/c)=\nabla(\varphi/c)\times\beta+(\varphi/c)\operatorname{curl}\beta$ ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]), and $\operatorname{curl}\beta=\nabla s\times\dot\beta$ by the coordinate formula applied to $\beta=z'(s(x,t))/c$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); substituting $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$ and $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$ gives $$B=-C\left[\frac{1-|\beta|^2+rd/c}{c\kappa D^2}\,n\times\beta+\frac{n\times\dot\beta}{c^2\kappa D}\right].$$ Crossing the displayed $E$ with $n/c$ gives this same expression by $n\times(n-\beta)=-n\times\beta$ and $D=\kappa r$, proving $B=n\times E/c$. before.title: Causal reachability, causal futures and pasts, causal diamonds, and reachability by future causal paths in affine Minkowski space
before.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and write Cbar^+ := cl(C^+) and Cbar^- := cl(C^-) for the closed future and past cones of the time orientation; these are the convex cones with Cbar^+ = C^+ union {0}, Cbar^- = C^- union {0} and Cbar^+ intersect Cbar^- = {0} (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets, lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components). This definition fixes the following objects. (a) Causal and chronological reachability. For events p,q in A set p <=q iff q - p is in Cbar^+ and p <q iff q - p is in C^+; the first is read 'q is causally reachable from p' and the second 'q is strictly (chronologically) reachable from p'. (b) Futures and pasts. J^+(p) := {q : p <= q} = p + Cbar^+, I^+(p) := {q : p < q} = p + C^+, J^-(p) := {q : q <= p} = p + Cbar^- and I^-(p) := {q : q < p} = p + C^-; p lies in J^+(p) intersect J^-(p) and in neither I^+(p) nor I^-(p). (c) Causal diamonds. For events p,q in A with p <= q the causal diamond of the ordered pair (p,q) is the set J^+(p) intersect J^-(q). (d) Reachability by future causal paths. A piecewise C^1 future causal path is a piecewise C^1 curve x: [a,b] -> A (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline) whose one-sided tangents at every point of [a,b] are future causal (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets). For events p,q in A say that q is reachable from p by a future causal path when p = q, or when p is not q and there are real numbers a < b and a piecewise C^1 future causal path x: [a,b] -> A with x(a) = p and x(b) = q; write R^+(p) for the set of events reachable from p in this sense. (e) Conventions and scope. All objects are defined from the affine structure, the form eta and the time orientation alone; no chart, origin, spatial orientation of V or unit convention enters. The statement asserts no property of these objects: the reflexivity of <= is (b), while transitivity of <=, the identification R^+(p) = J^+(p), the antisymmetry 'p <= q and q <= p imply p = q', the monotonicity of inertial coordinate time and the invariance under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps are proved later on this page (lem-sr-future-causal-sums-and-inertial-coordinate-criterion, thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence, lem-sr-spacelike-pairs-have-frame-dependent-time-order). No choice principle is used.
before.strategy: Definition item; the obligations are well-definedness of the new symbols. before.title: Parallel future null displacements compose to a future null displacement
before.statement: Worked computation in the chart x of an inertial frame. Let v := (1,1,0,0) and w := (2,2,0,0) be coordinate columns with respect to the basis of the frame. (a) v and w are future null: eta(v,v) = -1 + 1 = 0, eta(w,w) = -4 + 4 = 0, and both have positive time component; w = 2v, so the two directions are parallel. (b) The sum v + w = (3,3,0,0) is again future null, eta(v+w,v+w) = -9 + 9 = 0, and the endpoint q := x^{-1}(3,3,0,0) lies in J^+(p) for p := x^{-1}(0,0,0,0) but not in I^+(p), by the coordinate criterion; the straight path from p to q is a future null straight line of the model. (c) This is the boundary case of the sum clause: the sum of two future causal vectors is future causal, and it is future null exactly when the two vectors are positive multiples of one another, as here; by contrast the nonparallel pair of ex-sr-null-legs-compose-to-a-timelike-displacement has a timelike sum.

before.statement: Statement refuted: 'for any two distinct events p,q of the affine Minkowski model, the sign of the time-coordinate difference x^0(q) - x^0(p) is independent of the inertial frame.' Counterexample: in the chart x of an inertial frame let p := x^{-1}(0,0,0,0) and q := x^{-1}(11,13,0,0). Then q - p is spacelike (eta = 48 > 0) and, as computed in ex-sr-boost-makes-spacelike-events-simultaneous, the chart x_{3/5} of the frame related to x by the passive boost with parameter b = 3/5 gives x_{3/5}^0(q) - x_{3/5}^0(p) = 4 > 0, while the chart x_{12/13} of the frame related to x by the passive boost with parameter b = 12/13 gives x_{12/13}^0(q) - x_{12/13}^0(p) = -13/5 < 0. Both frames are inertial frames of the model and the two coordinate differences refer to the same pair of events, so the refuted statement is false. The counterexample does not touch causal pairs: by thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence(d) every inertial frame gives a positive time difference to a pair with q - p future causal, so the failure of frame independence is confined to spacelike-separated pairs.

after.title: Counterexample: the temporal order of a spacelike-separated pair is not the same in every inertial frame
after.statement: Statement refuted: 'for any two distinct events p,q of the affine Minkowski model, the sign of the time-coordinate difference x^0(q) - x^0(p) is independent of the inertial frame.' Counterexample: in the chart x of an inertial frame let p := x^{-1}(0,0,0,0) and q := x^{-1}(11,13,0,0). Then q - p is spacelike (eta = 48 > 0) and the chart x_{3/5} of the frame related to x by the passive boost with parameter b = 3/5 gives x_{3/5}^0(q) - x_{3/5}^0(p) = 4 > 0, while the chart x_{12/13} of the frame related to x by the passive boost with parameter b = 12/13 gives x_{12/13}^0(q) - x_{12/13}^0(p) = -13/5 < 0. Both frames are inertial frames of the model and the two coordinate differences refer to the same pair of events, so the refuted statement is false. The counterexample does not touch causal pairs: by thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence(d) every inertial frame gives a positive time difference to a pair with q - p future causal, so the failure of frame independence is confined to spacelike-separated pairs.
after.strategy: Use the passive boost formula x_b^0=gamma_b(x^0−b x^1) supplied by def-lorentz-boost. For b=3/5, gamma=5/4 and gamma(11−13b)=(5/4)(16/5)=4. For b=12/13, gamma=13/5 and gamma(11−13b)=−13/5. Each |b|<1, so the A lemma lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse supplies a proper orthochronous boost, hence an inertial chart by the A affine-frame construction. The displacement squared norm is −121+169=48>0. Opposite time signs refute the stated frame-independence assertion. The causal coordinate criterion retains positive time difference for nonzero future causal pairs. No worked example is a premise and no choice principle is used.
